narrative.h2: Latin video carries fashion, geography, and rhythm at the same weight

sections.heading: What latin looks like
sections.body: Latin MVs blur reggaeton's club energy with flamenco's drama and the open-air shoots of Mexican regional pop. Wardrobe is the loudest channel — couture mixed with streetwear, gold detail, cultural reference points worn deliberately. Settings move between coastal landscapes, urban rooftops, and constructed dreamscapes. The camera rarely sits still; it circles, cranes, swings. Edits ride the percussion, which means tight cuts on the dembow rhythm and breaths held during the melodic moments.

sections.heading: Reference points that actually work
sections.body: Bad Bunny's 'Tití Me Preguntó', directed by his longtime collaborator Stillz, shows how to mix Puerto Rican neighborhood reality with fashion-film polish. Rosalía's 'Saoko' and the broader Motomami era is a masterclass in stripped staging — white walls, motorcycles, full commitment to the concept. Karol G's 'PROVENZA' defined a softer, golden-hour Latin pop palette, while Peso Pluma's 'Ella Baila Sola' brought regional Mexicano into the global frame. Maluma, Feid, and Colin Tilley-directed crossover work carry the genre forward in different lanes. The shared rule: culture appears as setting, never as costume.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Anchor in a real place before anything else. 'Rooftop in San Juan at sunset, palms visible, distant ocean' gives Tunee a foundation that fashion and choreography can sit on top of. Specify wardrobe details — 'gold chains, white tank, baggy linen pants' — at the same level of detail as the location. Cut tight to the dembow on choruses, then let one long shot run during a verse for contrast. The genre rewards both density and breath.
